newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba says Tietmeyer sees no need to change rates.
newsitem.headline: Buba says Tietmeyer sees no need to change rates.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Tuesday declined to comment directly on a bout of renewed market speculation about imminent rate cuts in Germany, but pointed to earlier comments by its president Hans Tietmeyer that rates would remain steady in the short term.

In response to a Reuter query, chief Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber said the central bank had no direct comment on market talk, but said "I would draw your attention to recent comments by Mr. Tietmeyer in the Spiegel magazine, when he observed - I see no short term reason for another interest rate change."
Buba says Tietmeyer sees no need to change rates
The interview appeared in this week's edition of the Spiegel magazine, and Tietmeyer's comment was made in response to a question on whether German rates had bottomed out.

Tietmeyer said in that interview "I have not said that. I only see in the short term no reason for another interest rate change. We will however evaluate in the coming months whether interest rates are appropriate.

"But to take the wind out of the sails of some speculators in Anglo-Saxon markets who are betting on a move in the other direction, I see no reason to raise rates in the foreseeable future," Tietmeyer told the magazine.
The Bundesbank's policy-making council will meet on Thursday for its regularly scheduled bi-weekly meeting.
Some market speculation has arisen that the Bundesbank may ease short-term interest rates again as there currently seems to be no inflationary danger in Germany.

France has also called for lower German rates, but Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said on Monday that the central banks of Germany and France had not changed their opinions on monetary policy.
The Bundesbank last cut interest rates in August when it dropped 30 basis points off its main money market rate, the repo, to three percent.
In April, it cut its discount rate, the floor to interest rates, to a historical low of 2.5 percent and lowered its ceiling Lombard rate to 4.5 percent.
